12                             Plaintiff,                                     
                                        ORDER DENYING JOINT MOTION           
13  v.                                   TO STAY PENDING BANKRUPTCY           
                                        WITHOUT PREJUDICE                    
14  STEPHANIE ANDREWS, an individual;                                         

   LVL TECHNOLOGIES USA, INC.,                                               
15                                       (ECF No. 68)                         
   a corporation; and DOES 1 through 10,                                     
16  inclusive,                                                                
17                          Defendants.                                       
18  STEPHANIE ANDREWS, an individual,                                         

19                                                                            
                       Counterclaimant,                                      
20                                                                            
   v.                                                                        
21                                                                            

22  AZENTA, INC.,                                                             
                      Counterdefendant.                                      
23                                                                            

24                                                                            
25       Presently before the Court is a Joint Motion to Stay Pending Bankruptcy (“Joint 
26  Mot.,”  ECF  No.  68)  filed  by  Defendant/Counterclaimant  Stephanie  Andrews  and 
27  Plaintiff/Counterdefendant Azenta,  Inc.  (collectively,  the “Moving  Parties”).    For  the 
28  below reasons, the Court DENIES the Joint Motion WITHOUT PREJUDICE.       
1                              BACKGROUND                                    
2       This  case  involves  a  dispute  between  the  life-sciences  company  Azenta,  Inc. 
3  (“Plaintiff” or “Azenta”), Azenta’s former employee Stephanie Andrews (“Andrews”), and 
4  Andrews’ new employer LVL Technologies USA, Inc. (“LVL”).  See Compl. ¶¶ 1–6, ECF 
5  No. 1.  Azenta alleges that Andrews, while acting as an agent of LVL, misappropriated 
6  Azenta’s trade secrets.  Id.  Both Andrews and LVL have answered Azenta’s Complaint, 
7  see ECF Nos. 9, 12, and Andrews has asserted a counterclaim against Azenta for unpaid 
8  compensation, see ECF No. 12 at 29–36.                                    
9       All Parties participated in an Early Neutral Evaluation Conference on March 6, 2023, 
10  and a Case Management Conference on March 14, 2023.  See ECF Nos. 17, 19.  The Parties 
11  then began discovery.  See generally Docket.  On October 18, 2023, LVL indicated that it 
12  had filed a Chapter-11 petition in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the Middle 
13  District of Florida.  See ECF No. 58.  Because LVL’s Chapter-11 petition triggered an 
14  automatic stay pursuant to 11 U.S.C. § 362, Magistrate Judge Jill L. Burkhardt vacated the 
15  case’s schedule as to LVL but left it in place as to Andrews.  See ECF No. 59.   
16       The Moving Parties now ask the Court to stay this action in its entirety for 180 days.  
17  Joint Mot. at 2. The Moving Parties point out that Azenta continues to seek discovery 
18  responses and production from LVL, including documents that Azenta contends will help 
19  Azenta establish its damages.  Id. at 2–3.  Specifically, Azenta seeks “records related to 
20  Andrews’ sales to Azenta customers on behalf of LVL (both prior to and after leaving 
21  Azenta’s employ) and LVL’s profits.”  Id. at 3.  If those records exist, per the Moving 
22  Parties, they are in LVL’s possession.  Id.  In addition, Azenta contends that it cannot 
23  “determine the full scope of Andrews’ alleged misconduct” without conducting a forensic 
24  review of LVL’s systems and databases.  Id.  Because it cannot access important evidence, 
25  Azenta argues, the “bankruptcy stay does not just affect Azenta’s case against LVL, but 
26  also its case against Andrews.”  Id.  Proceeding under these circumstances, per the Moving 
27  Parties, would waste their and the Court’s resources.  See id.            
28  / / /                                                                     
1                            LEGAL STANDARD                                  
2       District  courts  have  “broad  discretion  to  stay  proceedings.”  Clinton  v.  Jones, 
3  520 U.S. 681, 706 (1997).  The Court may stay an action pending resolution of independent 
4  proceedings where “it is efficient for its own docket and the fairest course for the parties.”  
5  Leyva v. Certified Grocers of  Cal., Ltd., 593 F.2d 857, 863 (9th Cir. 1979).  When 
6  determining whether a stay is appropriate, the Court must consider (1) “the possible 
7  damage which may result from the granting of a stay,” (2) “the hardship or inequity which 
8  a  party  may  suffer  in  being  required  to  go  forward,”  and  (3)  “the  simplifying  or 
9  complicating of issues, proof, and questions of law which could be expected to result from 
10  a stay.”  CMAX, Inc. v. Hall, 300 F.2d 265, 268 (9th Cir. 1962).  “A stay should not be 
11  granted unless it appears likely the other proceedings will be concluded within a reasonable 
12  time  in  relation  to  the  urgency  of  the  claims  presented  to  the  court.”  
13  Leyva, 593 F.2d at 864.                                                   
14                                ANALYSIS                                    
15       The Moving Parties have not persuaded the Court that a stay is justified.  First, 
16  though the Moving Parties assert that they cannot access documents that may “help Azenta 
17  establish its damages,” Joint Mot. at 3, the Joint Motion does not demonstrate that without 
18  said documents, Azenta will suffer sufficient hardship or inequity to justify a stay of its 
19  case against Andrews.  Merely labeling certain document productions as “key” does not 
20  make them so, particularly where it appears that Azenta could use alternate means to 
21  acquire the information they seek.  For example, though Azenta may not be able to access 
22  LVL’s  records of  Andrews’ sales,  see  id.,  Azenta  could seek  additional  information 
23  regarding said sales from either Andrews or its own customers.  Absent a stronger showing 
24  of prejudice to Azenta’s ability to proceed against Andrews, the Court is disinclined to 
25  grant a stay.1  Cf. United States v. Dos Cabezas Corp., 995 F.2d 1486, 1491 n.3 (9th Cir. 
26                                                                            

27  1 The Parties appear to rely solely on the “hardship” prong of the stay analysis, as they do not argue—and 
28  the Court is not convinced—that a stay will “simplify issues, proof, and questions of law.”  CMAX, Inc., 
1  || 1993) (describing how some courts have refused to extend an automatic bankruptcy stay 
2         nonbankrupt  defendants  absent  a  showing  that  the  bankrupt  defendant  is  an 
3   ||indispensable party); Fed. Deposit Ins.  Corp. v. Appraisal Pac., Inc., No.  14-CV-0079-H- 
4   ||BLM, 2014 WL 12564365, at *1—2 (S.D. Cal. Sept.  17, 2014) (declining to stay an action 
5 || with respect to nonbankrupt parties where it appeared that the case could “proceed against 
6 || the [nonbankrupt defendant] without [the bankrupt defendants]’). 
7         Second,  it  is  not  clear  to  the  Court  that  it  is  “likely”  that  LVL’s  bankruptcy 
8 || proceedings “will be concluded within a reasonable time in relation to the urgency of the 
9 || claims presented to the [CJourt.”  See Leyva, 593 F.2d at 864.  Though the Moving Parties 
10 || ask for a 180-day stay, their request is “subject to the [Moving] Parties’ right to later seek 
11        extension of the stay.”  Joint Mot. at 4.  In truth, the Moving Parties seek a stay “pending 
12 || [the] outcome of [LVL’s] recently-filed bankruptcy petition.”  Jd. at 2.  The Court sees no 
13 || reason to believe that LVL will complete its bankruptcy proceeding within 180 □□□□□□  The 
14    uncertain,  potentially  lengthy  character  of the  Moving  Parties’  requested  stay  weighs 
15 || against granting the Moving Parties’ request.  See Levya, 593 F.2d at 864. 
16                                     CONCLUSION 
17         For the foregoing reasons, the Court DENIES the Moving Parties’ Joint Motion to 
18 || Stay Pending Bankruptcy (ECF No. 68).  The Court’s denial is WITHOUT PREJUDICE 
19 || to a renewed motion that cures the above-noted deficiencies. 
20         IT IS SO ORDERED. 
21     Dated:  December 15, 2023                       tt 
22                                            ja  Janis L. Sammartino
